title: Putin Has Run Out of Moves
gist: Russia is sliding into prolonged stagflation — sub-1% growth, 6%+ inflation, and a budget deficit ballooning to 2.8% of GDP — while Ukrainian long-range drone strikes hit energy infrastructure, and the only real fix (ending the war) is the option Putin is least likely to choose.

insights.claim: The broad consensus among Russia-watchers is that the country is facing a prolonged bout of stagflation, combining low growth with persistently high inflation.
insights.speaker: Anders Åslund
insights.so_what: A consensus stagflation call on Russia implies continued pressure on the ruble, real wages, and consumer demand, relevant for anyone tracking Russia-linked commodity flows or sanctions effectiveness.
insights.quote: The broad consensus among Russia-watchers is that the country is facing a prolonged bout of stagflation.

insights.claim: Russian economic growth in 2026 is unlikely to exceed 1%.
insights.speaker: Anders Åslund
insights.so_what: A sub-1% growth call sets a concrete benchmark to test against official Russian GDP releases and sanctions-impact models.
insights.quote: Growth this year is unlikely to exceed 1%

insights.claim: Russian inflation is stuck at 6% or higher, despite tightening pressures on the economy.
insights.speaker: Anders Åslund
insights.so_what: Persistent high inflation alongside a ballooning deficit points to continued central bank tightening risk and ruble volatility.
insights.quote: inflation is still stuck at 6% (or more)

insights.claim: President Vladimir Putin has abandoned fiscal caution and allowed Russia's government budget deficit to balloon to 2.8% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Anders Åslund
insights.so_what: A widening deficit under wartime spending pressure signals rising reliance on the National Wealth Fund or debt issuance, a leading indicator of Russian fiscal stress to monitor.
insights.quote: President Vladimir Putin has thrown fiscal caution to the wind and allowed the government’s budget deficit to balloon to 2.8% of GDP. It isn’t likely to end well.

insights.claim: Ukraine's relentless long-range drone strikes on Russian energy infrastructure are compounding Russia's economic distress alongside low growth and high inflation.
insights.speaker: Anders Åslund
insights.so_what: Continued drone strikes on refineries and energy assets are a direct supply-side drag on Russian export revenue and a factor to weigh in Russian oil/refined-product export forecasts.
insights.quote: Even with the Russian economy suffering from low growth, high inflation, and relentless Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on energy infrastructure

insights.claim: The most promising option for reviving the Russian economy — ending the war on Ukraine — is also the option least likely to be pursued, because it depends entirely on Putin's willingness to stop the war.
insights.speaker: Anders Åslund
insights.so_what: Implies Russia's economic recovery path is politically gated rather than policy-gated, meaning economic distress alone is unlikely to force a near-term war resolution.
insights.quote: the most promising option for reviving the economy is the least likely to be pursued, because it requires President Vladimir Putin’s willingness to end the war on Ukraine
